why.3: Converts 7.5 psig to about 208 inH2O and 160/165 inH2O to about 5.8/6.0 psig. It notes both thresholds are far below the setpoint and recommends a single unit.
why.4: Lists missing surge detection/anti-surge blow-off valve control and a minimum flow per blower to avoid surge. It also notes that simultaneous valve closures could deadhead the blowers into surge.
why.5: Flags auto-restart as hazardous: unexpected starts, backspin, simultaneous inrush tripping breakers, and skipped permissives. It proposes staggered starts, re-verified permissives and an operator-enable selection.
why.6: Item 7 is called out for lacking tags, setpoints, delays and a manual reset. For item 4, the output only notes the discharge valve lacks a tag. It never questions whether a 'discharge valve open' permissive fits centrifugal blower starting practice or says it needs confirming.

why.1: R-01 flags that a 'fixed setpoint' conflicts with most-open-valve reset of the setpoint. It gives one strategy: a reset setpoint with min/max clamps, rate limit and deadband, and a fixed setpoint only in manual or as the bad-PV fallback.
why.2: R-03 says closing the valve on DO loss starves the basin of air, the opposite of the stated intent. It proposes holding the last good valve output, raising an alarm, and excluding the basin from MOV logic.
why.3: R-02 converts 7.5 psig to about 208 inH2O and 160/165 inH2O to about 5.8/6.0 psig. It explains that the staging thresholds contradict the setpoint, so stage-off would always be true.
why.4: R-08 flags that surge and blow-off protection are undefined and asks for them in the blower module. R-03 notes that closing valves dead-heads the header and can surge the blowers.
why.5: R-04 flags simultaneous restart of all blowers (inrush, voltage sag, no permissive check). It proposes a staggered lead-order restart with an outage limit, operator prompting after long outages, and operations sign-off.
why.6: R-05 fully covers the missing vibration tag, value, delay and reset. But R-06 only notes the discharge valve lacks a tag and position switch. It never questions whether a 'discharge valve open' start permissive suits centrifugal blower starting practice, or asks for it to be confirmed.

why.1: F-03 flags that a 'fixed setpoint' contradicts the MOV reset. It states one strategy: 7.5 psig is the initial and maximum setpoint, with MOV trim below it within defined limits and rate (SP-002 to SP-005).
why.2: F-06 says closing the valve starves the biology, stops mixing and can dead-head the blowers. It proposes holding the last position, then a fixed fallback position, never fully closed. Section E adds an alarm for a bad AIT-90x signal.
why.3: F-01 converts 7.5 psig to about 208 inH2O and 160/165 inH2O to about 5.8/6.0 psig, and calls this a units conflict. F-02 explains that the staging thresholds and the setpoint do not agree, so staging cannot work.
why.4: F-05 flags missing surge and minimum-flow protection for the blowers. F-06 links valve closure to dead-heading the blowers, which covers the low-flow risk from valve closure.
why.5: F-10 flags that simultaneous restart causes inrush and voltage sag. FR-AER-030 to 033 propose a staggered restart (SP-020) with an outage limit and trip exclusion.
why.6: F-11 covers the missing vibration tags, value, delay, latch and reset. However, the output does not question the discharge-valve-open start permissive against typical centrifugal blower practice. It only notes the valve has no tag, and its proposed start sequence keeps 'open discharge valve' without asking for confirmation.

why.1: Calls out that the setpoint is described as both 'fixed at 7.5 psig' and MOV-reset, and that only one can be true. Recommends one strategy: a pressure setpoint that floats via MOV between defined minimum and maximum limits, with a slow reset rate.
why.2: States that closing the valve starves the basin of air, kills nitrification and can send it septic. Proposes holding the last good position or going to a defined fallback/minimum position with an alarm.
why.3: Converts 7.5 psig to about 208 inH2O and notes that 160/165 inH2O is about 5.8/6.0 psig, well below the setpoint. Explains that the stage-on and stage-off logic therefore fails, and asks for a single unit throughout.
why.4: Lists surge and minimum flow protection for multistage centrifugal blowers, requiring a blow-off or recirculation strategy and minimum turndown 'particularly as basin valves close down'. Also says the MOV minimum setpoint must keep the blowers out of surge.
why.5: Flags large inrush and possible generator or utility overload when all blowers restart together. Requires staggered restarts with defined delays and priority, a lockout until coast-down, and no auto-restart for tripped blowers.
why.6: Says the vibration trip needs sensor tags, separate alarm and trip setpoints, a trip delay and a latched trip with manual reset. For item 4, says the discharge valve strategy (open before start versus opened on a timer after start) must be confirmed with the blower vendor.

why.1: Explicitly flags the contradiction ('fixed setpoint' vs MOV reset), says 'Pick one', and states a clear strategy: use MOV reset, with 7.5 psig as the initial or maximum value, plus limits, rate, deadband and exclusions.
why.2: Says closing the valve causes under-aeration and risks a process upset and septic conditions. Proposes holding the last good output or a safe position, switching to a fixed airflow or position setpoint, and raising an alarm.
why.3: Converts 7.5 psig to about 208 inH2O and 160/165 inH2O to about 5.8/6.0 psig. Shows the staging thresholds don't fit the setpoint and asks for consistent units.
why.4: Flags missing surge protection (minimum flow limit, blow-off or bypass valve). It does not explicitly connect surge risk to MOV logic or basin valve closure reducing flow. The MOV/valve-closure point is framed only as driving header pressure incorrectly, and surge is mentioned for staging margin only.
why.5: Flags simultaneous restart as a hazard because of high inrush and repeat trips. Proposes a restoration delay, staggered sequenced restarts, permissive checks, and excluding blowers that were faulted before the outage.
why.6: Notes the vibration trip has no tags, setpoints, trip delay, or manual-reset lockout. For item 4, asks to confirm the open-discharge/closed-IGV starting condition against the blower vendor's requirements.

why.1: The output never flags PIC-501 vs PIC-510 as a possible tag inconsistency or ambiguity. D-03 assumes two controllers and asks to 'Define PIC-510 as a separate controller', so it adopts the second tag instead of asking for one defined tag/function.
why.2: D-04 says tripping K-501A/B at high-high removes the main pressure relief path. IL-01 and FR-TPC-022 hold the compressors at maximum load, keep PIC-510/flare in Auto and never trip on high-high. IL-02 trips the compressors on low-low pressure.
why.3: D-07 rejects 'low pressure is not a concern' and notes the compressors can pull the tank to vacuum. It adds PAL (80 mbarg) and PALL (40 mbarg) with a latched compressor trip (IL-02), both well above the -5 mbarg vacuum relief. It also adds a minimum load and a make-up gas open item.
why.4: D-06 flags the missing authorization, time limit and alarm, and the correction removes the HMI bypass in favor of a hardwired method under the site procedure. It never mentions compensating measures, which the expectation explicitly requires.
why.5: D-11 says the vendor reference is not a specification. FR-TPC-036 defines the signals exchanged (anti-surge active, vendor trip) and states the BPCS does not command the anti-surge valve, so ownership stays with the vendor. IL-03, the alarms and FR-TPC-033 define what the DCS does on a vendor trip.
why.6: An order check is given (SP-08 < ... < SP-05) and declared correct. Margins between the levels (e.g., 220 to 250 to 290 mbarg) are not assessed and no gaps are discussed, so the expectation is only partly addressed.

why.1: D-04 flags that PIC-510 is not tied to PIC-501, and D-13 flags inconsistent tag naming (PIC-510 has no PT, high-high has no tag). The corrected section gives each controller one defined tag, PV and function (PIC-501 for compressor capacity on the PT-501 median, PIC-510 for the flare valve on PT-510).
why.2: D-05 states that tripping the compressors on high-high removes the main means of lowering tank pressure when it is needed. FR-BOG-017 keeps the compressors at maximum load. Low-pressure stopping is added (CE-01, PALL). Flare/relief action is left to PIC-510/PV-512 and the SRS, and the PAHH operator response says to check PV-512 is open.
why.3: D-08 says the tank can be pulled to vacuum and adds PAL-501 at 60 mbarg (a limiter that reduces load to minimum) and PALL-501 at 25 mbarg (stops all K-501). Both sit above the -5 mbarg vacuum relief, and the ordering check confirms this.
why.4: D-07 flags the missing authority control, time limit, alarm and MOC/bypass procedure, and the bypass is corrected with a key switch, a 4 h limit and an alarm. Compensating measures during the bypass are never mentioned.
why.5: FR-BOG-024 to 026 state anti-surge behavior: minimum flow, valve fail-open, and priority over PIC-501. The interface itself is not defined: no signal list, no statement of who owns or controls the recycle valve, and nothing on what the DCS receives on a surge trip beyond a generic vendor trip list (OI-08).
why.6: An ordering check is given and D-10 notes the missing low-side stage. Margins between steps are not assessed: nothing is said about 220 to 250 mbarg (30 mbar) or 250 to 290 mbarg (40 mbar), or whether they are adequate. The output only states that the order holds.

why.1: Defect 9 flags the inconsistent tag naming (PIC-501 vs PIC-510 for the same variable). The corrected section then defines each tag explicitly: PIC-501 on PT-501 for normal compressor control, and PIC-510 on a separate PT-510 for flare relief.
why.2: Defect 2 says tripping the compressors at HH removes the primary vapor-removal and relief capacity just below the PSV set pressure. The corrected 6.2.4 keeps the compressors and flare in service and closes the pressure sources. The PSLL is the trip that stops the compressors.
why.3: Defect 1 calls the low-pressure/vacuum hazard critical. The corrected section adds PAL at 50, make-up gas at 70 and a PSLL at 20 mbarg that trips the compressors and closes PV-512, all above the -5 mbarg vacuum relief.
why.4: Defect 3 lists the missing access control, authorization record, time limit, alarm and compensating measures. Corrected 6.2.5 requires a key switch, supervisor permit, time limit, continuous alarm, logging and compensating measures, with no HMI-only bypass.
why.5: Defect 8 and corrected 6.2.8 require a defined interface. It covers the signals exchanged (run status, load, fault, recycle valve position), recycle cooling, how recycle interacts with PIC-501, and which package trips are hardwired to the SIS. This goes well beyond a one-line reference.
why.6: Defect 9 notes the missing ladder and the gap between 120 and 220 mbarg with no HI alarm. Defect 2 comments on the 40 mbar margin between HH and the PSV. The corrected section gives a full ladder from vacuum relief through normal, PAH, flare, HH and PSV.

why.1: The output never flags that PIC-501 and PIC-510 look like an inconsistent tag for the same tank pressure function, and never asks for one defined tag. It treats them as two separate controllers (defect 9, 'Control (PIC-501/510)') and keeps both in the corrected section.
why.2: Defect 1 says tripping the BOG compressors at high-high removes pressure relief exactly when it is needed. The corrected 6.2.3 keeps the compressors running and PV-512 available to flare, and 6.2.5 trips the compressors on PALL instead.
why.3: Defect 3 rates dismissing low pressure as Critical, noting the vacuum risk and the small -5 mbarg margin. The corrected 6.2.5 adds PAL at [70], make-up gas at [50] and a PALL at [30] that trips the compressors, all before the -5 mbarg vacuum relief point.
why.4: Defect 2 flags the HMI bypass as having no authorization, time limit, alarm or independence. The corrected 6.2.4 requires a key switch, work permit, time limit, alarm and logging, and per-transmitter bypass so the remaining voting stays active as a compensating measure.
why.5: Defect 6 and the corrected 6.2.7 define the interface. The vendor provides a fail-open recycle valve and cooler. It exposes surge margin, recycle valve position, compressor status/trip and the minimum-flow limit to the DCS, and the interaction with PIC-501 is specified.
why.6: The output builds a setpoint ladder (6.2.8) running from vacuum relief through normal control, PAH, flare, PAHH and PSV. It comments on the PSV margin against the unstated design pressure and accumulation, and flags the missing ladder and the flare hysteresis as gaps.

why.1: F-01 says a standard PLC input (I:3/0) cannot be the E-stop function and notes no stop category or reset. It requires a hardwired or safety-rated circuit that removes drive power, with I:3/0 as status only. Stop category and PL go to the SRS (OI-02), and the latched reset path is defined (F-02, FR-CP3-017).
why.2: F-03 calls the auto-resume an unexpected-restart hazard. It removes auto-resume and requires going to Stopped, then Reset and Start after the doors close (FR-CP3-016, with a FAT test confirming no motion).
why.3: F-05 and the state table map downstream full and infeed starved to Suspended, and operator Stop to Stopping/Stopped. Held is reserved for jam, photoeye fault, or operator Hold.
why.4: F-08 notes there is no time qualifier and that product blocks PE-320 in normal flow, and adds a blocked-time delay (SP-CP3-003 = 3 s). However, the threshold is a fixed provisional value and is never related to machine speed or rate.
why.5: FR-CP3-014 sends starvation to Suspended, with automatic Unsuspending once bottles are present for SP-CP3-006. This is explicitly auto-reset, in contrast to the latched Held/jam fault that needs Alarm Reset and Unhold.
why.6: F-09 flags that the 30 cases/min is a fixed prose value with no tolerance or adjustability. Section 2.9 says operators cannot change setpoints and changes go through MOC. OI-05 raises the conveyor speed relation to case rate. Ramp behavior is not addressed, but the core deficiency is flagged.

why.1: F-01 says a standard PLC input is not a safety function and requires the E-stop to be hardwired to a safety relay or safety PLC, keeping I:3/0 for status only. F-02 flags that the stop category and reset are undefined. It requires a manual reset followed by Clear and Reset, and OI-01 assigns the stop-category definition in the SRS to an owner.
why.2: F-03 names automatic resume after the doors close as an unexpected-restart hazard. It requires the machine to stay Held until a deliberate START (FR-CP3-005), and the FAT test checks for no motion after the doors close.
why.3: F-05 and F-08 map outfeed full and starvation to Suspended. F-06 corrects operator Stop to Stopping, then Stopped. F-05 states that Held is for internal or operator-initiated conditions. The state table puts jam, HOLD and door open under Holding.
why.4: F-09 notes there is no blocked time, so every passing case would read as a jam. It adds SP-CP3-05 as the blocked-time threshold, which the setpoint list says to confirm against case length and speed.
why.5: FR-CP3-007 and IL-04 define starvation as Suspended with automatic return to Execute once bottles are present for SP-CP3-02. This is distinct from the latched jam and drive faults (IL-05, IL-06), which need START or RESET.
why.6: F-10 flags that 30 cases/min is a single value with no nominal/maximum definition, range, tolerance or ramp, and OI-04 asks for rate limits and ramp. Section 9 states the operator may change the rate within limits. Interaction with upstream and downstream speed is not explicitly flagged, but the missing ramp and limits are flagged concretely.

why.1: Finding 1 says the E-stop depends on a standard PLC input and software. It requires a hardwired dual-channel safety relay or safety PLC with STO, independent of the PLC. Section 1.1 specifies a Stop Category [0/1], a latching E-stop, and an explicit Reset then Start.
why.2: Finding 3 calls auto-resume an unexpected-restart hazard and requires a deliberate reset and start. Section 1.2 states that closing the doors does not restart the machine and that a Safety Reset plus Start is needed.
why.3: Finding 4 and Section 2 map downstream full and infeed starved to Suspended (external conditions). Operator Stop goes to Stopping → Stopped. Held is for operator Hold commands or machine-internal conditions.
why.4: Finding 6 notes there is no time qualifier, so a normal passing case would trip the jam. Section 4 defines a continuous-blocked threshold that is adjustable and longer than the longest normal case transit time, which ties it to rate.
why.5: Section 3 sends starvation to Suspended with automatic resume once PE-310 is stable for [x s]. Sensor faults raise a separate alarm. This is contrasted with Held/Stopped conditions that require operator acknowledge or Reset plus Start.
why.6: Finding 7 flags the single 30 cpm figure with no tolerance, max, ramp, or relation to the conveyors. Section 5 adds conveyor speed following, ramp times, and rate changes restricted to authorized users via the HMI.

why.1: Item 1 says a standard PLC input and program logic is not a safety function. It requires a safety relay or safety PLC, notes the missing stop category and the missing manual reset requirement. Rev B section 2.1 specifies Stop Category 0/1, latching, and a manual safety reset.
why.2: Item 2 calls automatic restart on door close a restart hazard and requires a deliberate reset and start. Section 2.2 states that closing the doors does not restart the machine and that a safety reset, then Reset and Start, are required.
why.3: Item 3 and section 3 correct the state usage. Suspended is for external conditions (downstream blocked, upstream starved), and downstream full maps to Suspending/Suspended. Operator Stop goes to Stopping/Stopped. Held is for internal equipment conditions.
why.4: The output correctly flags that there is no time filter, so a normal case passing would trigger a jam. It defines a placeholder blocked-time threshold [x s, adjustable] with qualifying conditions. However, it never ties that threshold to machine speed or case transit time, which the expectation explicitly requires.
why.5: Section 4.1 makes starvation a Suspended state with a non-latching message. It auto-resumes once bottle flow is re-established for [x s or y bottles]. This contrasts with the jam case in 4.3, which has a latching alarm and requires manual clearing and Reset/Unhold.
why.6: Item 6 flags that 30 cases/min is not defined as nominal, maximum or setpoint, and that adjustability, conveyor speed relationships and ramps are missing. Section 4.4 adds placeholders for the adjustment range, speed matching and ramps. It does not explicitly address who is authorized to change the speed, but the core points are covered.

why.1: R-06 flags that there is no purge or crank-purge before fuel and ignition. It adds a purge step with a minimum crank time (SP-05) before fuel admission. Revised Step 2 requires purge time of at least SP-05 at purge speed.
why.2: R-07 flags the missing timeouts and failure responses, naming failure to light and hung start. The revised step table gives each step a timeout and a failure response. Step 3 on failed light-off is 'Close fuel. Re-purge.' before retry. Step 4 trips on a hung start or failure to reach idle.
why.3: R-02 marks fail-closed blowdown valves as Critical because ESD could not depressurize on loss of power or air. It proposes fail-open, and the cause-and-effect row opens the blowdown valves. It leaves a hedge (fail-closed only with an accumulator and a hazard-analysis basis, OI-01), but the correction toward fail-open is clearly proposed.
why.4: R-01 and FR-U2-020 reject auto-restart. They require ESD-LOCKOUT, local verification (cause may be unverified), a manual reset, and a new operator Start command. The cause-and-effect table states 'Local manual reset after verification'.
why.5: R-04 rejects 'see vendor data' as a reference, not a specification. R-05 flags the missing delay, voting and sensor-failure handling. Values go into one setpoint list (SP-01, SP-03, SP-04), and FR-U2-014 to 016 define the delay and the 2oo2/1oo1 voting.
why.6: R-09 calls recycle closure at idle premature, requires a surge-margin check, and requires a ramped close under anti-surge control. R-03 questions ESD logic in the same PLC as unit control, cites IEC 61511 SIS/BPCS independence, and asks for the boundary to be defined.

why.1: F-08 flags the missing purge crank before fuel admission and the explosion risk. Start step 2 adds a purge crank at purge speed for a set time (SP-U2-003), confirmed against the vendor purge requirement.
why.2: F-06 states there are no timeouts or failure responses. The step table gives every step a timeout and a failure response, covering failed ignition and hung start (failure to reach idle). Step 3 requires a new purge before any retry.
why.3: F-02 states that fail-closed blowdown valves trap gas and that blowdown valves normally fail open. It specifies fail-open, and the fail-position table shows the blowdown valves as Open, replacing fail-closed.
why.4: F-01 rejects auto-restart and requires a latched ESD, reset only at the local panel after a field check, and a new operator Start. FR-U2-020 and FR-U2-021 codify this, with a test.
why.5: F-03 rejects 'trip value see vendor data' and requires the values in the setpoint list. FR-U2-014 defines the trip logic (either VT above SP-U2-010 for delay SP-U2-011), and FR-U2-017 covers bad-quality voting. SP-U2-010 is a single controlled entry, with an open item to enter the number.
why.6: F-09 flags recycle closure at idle with no permissive and no surge-control interaction, and requires closure under the anti-surge controller. F-05 questions the ESD sharing the unit PLC, asks for SIF/SIL status, references the IEC 61511 SRS, and requires confirmation of independence from the BPCS.

why.1: Item 3 flags that the sequence goes from cranking straight to fuel and ignition. It requires a timed purge or crank cycle that moves several volumes of air through the exhaust and enclosure before fuel is admitted, and gates fuel admission on it.
why.2: Item 6 flags that no step has a timeout or failure path. It covers case pressure never equalizing and failure to light (fuel shutoff, re-purge, limit on attempts). It also requires time and EGT limits on starter disengagement and acceleration, and a time limit to idle.
why.3: Item 2 states that fail-closed blowdown defeats the ESD on loss of power, air or signal, and that fail-open is the usual choice. It asks for the design intent to be confirmed as a possible typo. The output does allow a documented, risk-assessed alternative with stored energy, but the correction toward fail-open is clear.
why.4: Item 1 says the automatic restart should be removed and rejects throughput as a reason. It requires a manual ESD reset, a field check or acknowledgment because no one has inspected the station, and a fresh operator Start through the full permissive chain.
why.5: Item 9 says 'see vendor data' isn't a control specification. It requires stated alarm and trip setpoints, time delays, start-up masking, 1oo2/2oo2 voting for VT-2201/2202, and sensor fault handling.
why.6: Item 7 questions closing the recycle valve at idle and notes that anti-surge control is missing. It says recycle should stay open or under surge control during loading. Item 4 asks whether the ESD runs on a safety-rated independent PLC or shares a processor with unit control, and requires a SIL basis and a hardwired backup if shared.

why.1: Item 2 flags the missing gas-path purge before ignition in Step 3. It asks for a purge (crank) period of sufficient duration or volume changes before fuel admission, plus fuel valve proving and a trial-for-ignition timeout.
why.2: Item 9 says each step needs a timeout and abort action and lists per-step gaps (failure-to-light action, self-sustaining speed, acceleration timeout). It only asks for these to be defined rather than supplying them, and it never mentions purging before an ignition retry, which the expectation explicitly requires.
why.3: Item 3 notes that fail-closed blowdown valves prevent depressurization, which is the opposite of what ESD expects. It then hedges that this may be deliberate and asks only for a rationale; it never states the valves should fail open, so no correction is made.
why.4: Item 1 rejects automatic restart after ESD. It requires a deliberate manual ESD reset after the cause is investigated and cleared, re-established permissives, and a fresh operator Start command.
why.5: Item 7 states that 'see vendor data' is not acceptable. It requires alarm and trip setpoints, delay, 1oo2/2oo2 voting between VT-2201 and VT-2202, and handling of a bad-quality transmitter.
why.6: The same-PLC concern is well covered in item 4 (independence, SIL, safety-rated hardware). On the recycle valve, item 10 only calls the closure at idle 'vague' and asks that anti-surge control be stated as active; it never explicitly flags that closing the valve immediately at idle risks surge.

why.1: R-01 and the summary time budget (3 s + 6-8 s crank + 5 s stabilization + sync, giving about 15-25 s) show the 10 s limit is violated. The fix transfers ATS-L and ATS-C as soon as the first generator closes to the dead bus (sequence step 4).
why.2: Simultaneous transfer is replaced by a defined order. ATS-L and ATS-C transfer first, on the first generator. ATS-E transfers after the second generator parallels plus SP-08, or by delayed-automatic SP-09. The retransfer order is also defined (ATS-E, ATS-C, ATS-L).
why.3: R-08 and section 3.5 replace 'as required' with a defined priority (shed ATS-E first, never shed ATS-L or ATS-C). Triggers are concrete: SINGLE-GEN state, bus underfrequency SP-10 (58 Hz / 2 s) and generator overload SP-15 (100 % / 5 s). Restore is defined as a latched shed with operator reset after the second generator is back in PARALLEL. ATS-E is the only shed block, so the add-back order is a single defined step.
why.4: R-10 and SP-11 add a 15 min utility-stable timer before retransfer. R-12 and SP-12 add a 5 min unloaded cooldown before stop. Both appear in the retransfer sequence table.
why.5: R-13 and R-14 change low coolant temperature and low fuel to alarms only, citing NFPA 110 Level 1 Table 5.6.5.2. Table 3.6 keeps only overcrank, overspeed, low lube oil pressure, high coolant temperature and remote E-stop as shutdowns.
why.6: R-02 flags the conflict between 'start immediately' in 3.1 and the 3 s confirmation delay in 3.2. It resolves this with one start condition tied to setpoint SP-01.

why.1: F-01 shows that 3 s + 5 s already uses 8 of the 10 s before engine start and synchronizing. It fixes this by transferring ATS-L and ATS-C as soon as the first generator closes to the dead bus (step 4, FR-EPS-004).
why.2: F-02 replaces the simultaneous transfer with staged transfers. ATS-L and ATS-C go first. ATS-E follows after SP-10 and after the second generator closes (steps 4-6, FR-EPS-007). The load priority table sets P1 ATS-L, P2 ATS-C, P3 ATS-E.
why.3: Section 3.4 gives a priority table (ATS-L never shed, ATS-E shed first, then ATS-C). Triggers are bus kW above SP-14 and underfrequency below SP-15. FR-EPS-022 restores shed loads in stages, SP-10 apart, after the second generator closes. The restore order follows the priority list, with ATS-E sub-block order assigned to OI-02.
why.4: F-11 and SP-11 add a 30-minute retransfer delay, with a bypass if the emergency source fails. SP-13 adds a 5-minute unloaded cooldown before engine stop (steps R1-R4).
why.5: F-14 and F-15 make low coolant temperature and low fuel alarm-only. F-15 cites NFPA 110 Level 1 as the basis. The cause-and-effect table keeps overcrank, overspeed, low lube oil pressure, high coolant temperature and E-stop as shutdowns (F-16).
why.6: F-03 flags that 'immediately' contradicts the 3 s confirmation. It resolves this into one statement: start after the SP-01 delay.

why.1: Tallies 3 s + crank + 5 s stabilization + sync, roughly 16–28 s, which exceeds the 10 s requirement. Requires ATS-L and ATS-C to transfer as soon as the first generator closes to the bus.
why.2: Rejects simultaneous transfer and stages ATS-L, then ATS-C, then ATS-E. Equipment branch transfers after the second generator is paralleled or on a timed delay.
why.3: Calls 'sheds load as required' not a specification. Gives a load priority table and an underfrequency/overload shed trigger. Requires load-add sequencing in priority steps with time delays, and re-adding loads on recovery.
why.4: Requires an adjustable retransfer delay (5–30 min, ≥5 min typical) after utility is verified stable. Adds an unloaded cooldown (about 5 min) before stop and return to Auto.
why.5: Table makes low coolant temperature and low fuel alarm-only. Limits shutdowns to overspeed, low oil pressure, high coolant temperature, overcrank and E-stop. Cites NFPA 110 Level 1 as the basis.
why.6: Recommends shortening the 3 s delay to about 1 s, but never points out that 3.1's 'starts both generators immediately' contradicts the 3 s confirmation delay in 3.2.

why.1: Finding 1 adds up 3 s + crank + 5 s stabilization + sync to about 15–25 s, against the 10 s limit. Its fix is to transfer ATS-L and ATS-C immediately when the first generator closes to the dead bus.
why.2: Finding 2 and the rewrite drop simultaneous transfer. ATS-L and ATS-C go first, and ATS-E transfers later with a delay, after both units are online or after a timeout. Life safety and critical transfer together as top priority rather than one after the other, but the equipment branch is clearly delayed.
why.3: Finding 5 gives triggers (under-frequency, overload, failure to start or sync) and a rough priority (L/C never shed, E shed in blocks). It does not define a load-add order; it only says to 'define what happens when the second generator comes online,' and the rewrite says 'adds load in priority steps' without giving the order.
why.4: Finding 4 specifies an adjustable retransfer delay, typically 30 min and at least 5 min. It also specifies an unloaded cooldown of about 5 min before stopping.
why.5: Finding 3 says low coolant temperature and low fuel should be alarms only under NFPA 110. It keeps high coolant temperature and lists overspeed, low oil pressure, overcrank and high engine temperature as shutdowns, citing NFPA 110 Table 5.6.5.2 for Level 1.
why.6: The output suggests cutting the confirmation delay to 1 s but never points out that 3.1's 'starts both generators immediately' contradicts 3.2's 3 s confirmation delay, and does not reconcile the two statements.

why.1: F-02 marks this critical. Waiting for both generators (confirm delay, start, SP-05 stabilization, sync) cannot meet the 10 s SP-02 deadline. The fix transfers ATS-L and ATS-C on the first generator at the bus and synchronizes the second afterward.
why.2: F-03 replaces simultaneous transfer with a staged order: ATS-L, then ATS-C, then ATS-E after an SP-07 delay, with load-acceptance checks between steps. The corrected sequence outline repeats this order.
why.3: F-08 gives a kW trigger (SP-11, 1350 kW) and a partial priority ('shed ATS-E loads first, never ATS-L'). It defers the actual priority list to an open item. Restore is only 'manually or after SP-12', with no defined order for adding load back.
why.4: F-10 replaces immediate retransfer with a utility-stable delay (SP-08, 300 s). It adds an unloaded cooldown (SP-09, 300 s) before stopping and handles re-start on a second utility loss during cooldown.
why.5: F-11 and F-12 correctly make low fuel and low coolant temperature alarms only. F-14 lists overspeed, overcrank and low oil pressure but defers which are shutdowns ('Say which are shutdowns and which are alarms'). It does not commit to a limited permitted shutdown set or tie that set to an applicable code basis.
why.6: F-01 notes that 'starts immediately' contradicts the 3 s confirmation delay. It requires one start trigger, with the 10 s measured from utility loss including SP-01.

why.1: F-02 shows that the confirm delay, start, 5 s stabilization and second-generator sync together push transfer past 10 s. It fixes this by transferring ATS-L and ATS-C on the first generator to close to the bus, with the second generator as an add-on.
why.2: F-04 sets the order ATS-L, then ATS-C, then ATS-E after the SP-05 delay, each in its own step. Proposed sequence step 6 transfers ATS-E only after capacity is available, after the second generator syncs.
why.3: F-09 gives a shed priority (ATS-E first, then non-essential ATS-C, never ATS-L) and a kW trigger (SP-10). For restoring load it gives only a 'restore deadband and a restore delay', not a defined order for adding loads back. F-10's 'connect in order' is too vague to count as a restore order.
why.4: F-11 adds a stable-utility timer before retransfer (SP-08, 300 s). F-12 adds an unloaded cooldown before stopping (SP-09, 300 s). Both replace the immediate retransfer and stop.
why.5: F-13 changes low coolant temperature and low fuel to alarms only and explains why. It keeps shutdowns limited to overspeed, overcrank and manual emergency stop per NFPA 110 Level 1, with any high coolant temperature trip subject to AHJ approval. That states the code basis.
why.6: F-01 flags that 3.1 says 'immediately' while 3.2 starts the generators after the utility-loss delay. It fixes this with a single trigger: start on confirmed utility loss, delay per SP-02.

why.1: Finding 1 adds up the delays: 3 s confirmation, 6-10 s crank, 5 s stabilization, then the second generator's sync. That reaches about 15-20 s, past the 10 s limit. Finding 2 identifies the both-generators gate as the cause. The fix transfers ATS-L and ATS-C as soon as the first generator closes to the bus, and G-2 syncs in afterwards.
why.2: Finding 4 rejects simultaneous transfer. Life safety and critical transfer first, onto the first generator. The equipment branch is then load-stepped afterwards with timers and a capacity permissive (rewrite step 4). Life safety and critical are grouped together rather than strictly ordered, but the equipment branch clearly comes later.
why.3: The shedding priority is defined: equipment branch first, then non-essential loads, and life safety and critical are never shed. However, the trigger thresholds (kW, frequency, or breaker status) are only listed as things to specify, not actually defined. The order for adding load back is also not defined; 'restoration logic' is only listed as missing.
why.4: Finding 6 and rewrite step 6 add a stable-utility timer of 5-30 min before retransfer. They also add an unloaded cooldown run of about 5 min before the generators stop.
why.5: It correctly flags low coolant temperature and low fuel as alarms, not shutdowns, and cites NFPA 110 and the AHJ as the basis. However, its proposed shutdown set is overspeed, overcrank, and electrical faults only. It explicitly limits shutdowns to that set and leaves out low oil pressure, a standard required engine shutdown. The retained shutdown set is therefore incorrect.
why.6: Finding 7 explicitly notes that 3.1 says 'starts immediately' while 3.2 says 'after 3 s confirmation.' It says to pick one, and rewrite step 1 resolves it with a single defined short confirmation timer before the start signal.

why.1: Critical issue 1 adds up the 3 s delay, start time, 5 s stabilization and synchronizing, and shows this exceeds the 10 s requirement. Its fix is that the first ready generator closes to the dead bus and ATS-L and ATS-C transfer immediately.
why.2: Issue 3 replaces simultaneous transfer: ATS-L and ATS-C transfer first, then ATS-E is added in timed or capacity-checked steps. The revised outline puts ATS-E after the second generator syncs. Life safety and critical go together rather than strictly in sequence, but the equipment branch is clearly later.
why.3: Issue 7 calls 'as required' unimplementable. It requires a priority list, shed thresholds in kW or frequency, life safety never shed, and a defined restore order, including re-adding loads when the second generator returns.
why.4: Issue 6 adds a utility-return qualification timer of several minutes to 30, staged retransfer, and an unloaded cooldown of about 5 minutes before stopping, replacing immediate retransfer and stop.
why.5: It correctly makes low coolant temperature and low fuel alarms, citing NFPA 110. However, it also demotes high coolant temperature to an alarm and lists low oil pressure only as an alarm. NFPA 110 Level 1 practice keeps these as engine shutdowns, so the retained shutdown list (overspeed, overcrank, e-stop) does not match the expected permitted set.
why.6: Under smaller items it flags the 3.1 vs 3.2 contradiction ('start immediately' versus 'after 3 s delay'). It resolves it with a 0.5-3 s ride-through delay, measures the 10 s clock from actual utility loss, and carries this into the revised outline.

why.1: Section 2 (FR-EM) defines the modes Out of Service, Manual and Auto, plus command sources, once for all modules. Sections 3.2–3.3 and 4.2–4.3 define states, entry conditions, allowed exits and sequences once per class (PMP, VLV). The rules in section 1 and the note in section 5 say instance sheets never restate class requirements.
why.2: START FAIL and STOP FAIL use timeouts SP-PMP-01, -02 and -03. Valve TRAVEL FAIL uses SP-VLV-01 and -02. POSITION INVALID and POSITION LOST use SP-VLV-03. DRV_FAULT is a latched trip with coast stop. Unexpected stop, run without command and comm fail are also defined. Actions are given in the sequence failure responses and FRs, resets in the 3.5 interlock table and FR-EM-004 / FR-VLV-006.
why.3: Power restoration is covered: FR-EM-006 says outputs go to the fail position, mode and latched faults are kept, and there is no auto-restart. Mode transfer is not: nothing says what happens to a running pump or open valve when switching Manual to Auto or back. Nothing says whether the speed reference transfers bumplessly; FR-PMP-041 only names the speed source in each mode.
why.4: Section 5 gives an instance sheet template: header, options, tags, setpoint overrides, instance interlocks, alarm bindings, deviations as FR-<tag>-NNN, FAT checklist and open items. Section 6 fills it for P-4021 with data and deltas only.
why.5: P-4021 gives a start permissive of 30 kPa(g), a low-low trip of 15 kPa(g) and a 3 s trip delay that applies in STARTING and RUNNING. The action is a latched DRY RUN trip with coast stop, reset only after pressure recovers plus an operator Reset. The VFD speed source is set by FR-PMP-041 (operator setpoint in Manual, parent in Auto), with min/max clamps, a default manual speed and ramps. Generic pump behavior is referenced by FR ID, not restated. Caveat: there is a trip delay but no separate post-start bypass delay.
why.6: Section 1 ties the class revision to the PLC library version and requires MOC for class changes. Affected tags are found by querying the instance register's class column. Type tests are repeated per library version. Deviations must be explicit IDs, keeping a single source for common behavior.

why.1: CLS-PMP and CLS-VLV define modes (Auto/Manual/OOS), states, start/stop and open/close commands, and transitions with IDs. The P-4021 instance sheet says 'Behavior: CLS-PMP rev A' and lists requirement IDs instead of restating behavior.
why.2: Pump faults are defined with timing setpoints: fail to start (SP-PMP-02), fail to stop (SP-PMP-04), run feedback lost, drive fault and drive comms loss (SP-PMP-05). Valve faults cover fail to open/close (SP-VLV-01/02) and discrepancy (SP-VLV-03). Actions are TRIPPED/FAULTED with alarms, and resets are covered by FR-PMP-049 (operator only, latched) and FR-VLV-015.
why.3: FR-PMP-018 says Auto↔Manual keeps the state and the last speed setpoint, so the transfer is bumpless; valves follow the same rule. Power restoration is covered by FR-PMP-072 (stopped, mode retained, no auto start, start-edge rule FR-PMP-017) and FR-VLV-017 (rest position, commands cleared).
why.4: The instance sheet holds only tag data: tag, variant, drive tag, feedback source, enabled features (permissives), parent, setpoints/timers in C2, extra interlock rows (none) and an explicit deviations field (none). A2/B2 define this record format, generated from the tag database.
why.5: P-4021 gives a PT-4022 trip value of 0.3 bar g, a 3 s trip delay, a 10 s start mask after the run command, and an OK value for the permissive. The action is a latched DRY RUN trip, by reference to FR-PMP-040 and in the checkout. The auto speed setpoint source is the parent CIP circuit module, with min speed and ramps given. Generic behavior is referenced, not restated.
why.6: Class changes go through MOC with revision and change log. The tag database is queried to list affected instances. Instances are regenerated rather than copied, and repeated deviations are promoted to class options via MOC. The class is the single source with one type test per revision.

why.1: The Layer 1 class narrative is written once per class (EM-PUMP-VFD, EM-PUMP-DOL, EM-VALVE-ONOFF) and covers modes (Auto/Manual/Out of Service), states (Stopped/Starting/Running/Stopping/Faulted), commands and arbitration. Rule 1 says instance documents cite class clauses and never restate them, and the P-4021 sheet does this. Transitions are only implied by the state list, but the intent is clearly met.
why.2: Faults are only named as skeleton headings: run feedback timeout, unexpected start/stop, VFD ready/fault, speed deviation, and a valve open/close FB timeout column. No actions or resets are defined for them. Valve position discrepancy is not covered, and fail-to-stop is not explicit. Only the instance-specific dry-run trips get actions and resets.
why.3: Mode transfer behavior (manual to auto, bumpless outputs) and behavior after power restoration are not addressed anywhere.
why.4: The instance sheet template has sections for identification, I/O, parameters (non-default values marked), an interlock table (permissive/trip, delay, reset, bypass) and an explicit deviations section. The valves get a one-row-per-valve table.
why.5: Pressure values (0.3 bar permissive, 0.15 bar trip), a 3 s delay, the trip action and the speed source (CIP circuit phase) are documented without restating generic behavior. However, there is no delay after start (a start-up bypass while suction pressure establishes). The 3 s is only a trip debounce, so this element is missing.
why.6: Change control is addressed: stable clause IDs that are never reused, version changes on revision, instances citing class and version, deviations requiring approval, recurring deviations promoted into library change requests, and instance sheets generated from the PLC data source.

why.1: The class narrative defines modes (Auto, Manual, Out of Service) and lists commands, and the P-4021 text references the class instead of restating it. However, states and transitions are named only as headings; no state model or transition rules are actually defined.
why.2: It mentions start-confirmation timeout, unexpected-stop detection, drive fault, comms loss, feedback mismatch and valve travel-time supervision, with timers as parameters. Fail-to-stop is missing, and actions and resets per fault are left as a heading ('Which faults latch, and what resets them') rather than defined.
why.3: Power-up behavior is addressed ('does not auto-restart unless stated'). Mode transfer (manual to auto, bumpless output behavior) is not specified anywhere.
why.4: It provides an instance sheet template and a filled P-4021 table with tag, I/O, timers, permissives, interlocks, alarm changes, and an 'Exceptions to class' field that defaults to 'None'.
why.5: Dry-run protection is well documented: PT-4022 < 0.15 bar, a 10 s start-up bypass, a 3 s trip delay, and stop-and-latch with operator reset, without restating generic behavior. However, the VFD speed setpoint source is never stated; only speed limits and a TBC speed-ref I/O are given.
why.6: The class narrative is versioned and tied to the PLC library version, and a library upgrade triggers review. The brewery owns the class narratives and changes go through the standards owner. Restating class behavior is prohibited, and repeated exceptions are promoted to new class variants.
